metadata.scope: Independent introductory-to-applied companion with 50 original lessons and 150 original questions across the five topical courses in the 2026 public syllabus. Topic-level coverage of 23 syllabus modules is mapped, but this does not reproduce or replace the official curriculum, every learning outcome, exam questions or certification. Not CFA Level I preparation or a pass guarantee. US account glossary extends beyond the certificate. Educational only, not investment, legal or tax advice.
metadata.assessmentNote: Official program page describes 100 multiple-choice final-assessment questions and two attempts; app practice is separate.
metadata.curriculumNote: Older documents list six courses; this map follows the five topical courses in the current 2026 public syllabus. Confirm your enrolled version.

modules.title: The investment ecosystem
modules.summary: Follow capital from savers to productive uses, and understand who does what.
objectives: Distinguish investment, trading, custody and oversight roles
Connect operational work to investor trust

lessons.title: Follow the money
lessons.body: Investors supply capital. Issuers seek financing. Intermediaries connect them, while asset managers make portfolio decisions under a mandate. Custodians safeguard assets and maintain records. A single organization may perform several functions, but the obligations remain distinct.
lessons.example: A pension plan supplies capital through a bond purchase; the manager decides, a broker executes and a custodian holds the asset.

lessons.title: Why structure matters
lessons.body: Front-office decisions depend on operations, technology, legal, compliance and client service. A trade is not finished when a portfolio manager chooses it: execution, reconciliation and settlement must also work. In a product change, ask which records, disclosures and downstream systems depend on the change.
lessons.example: A fund-name change can affect prospectuses, records, websites and statements; one corrected document does not prove every output is updated.

lessons.title: Ethics before shortcuts
lessons.body: An action can be legal yet misleading or unfair. Identify affected stakeholders, incentives, relevant rules and alternatives before acting. Disclose and manage conflicts rather than assuming disclosure fixes everything. Protect confidential information and escalate uncertainty through approved channels.
lessons.example: A recommendation pays the adviser more than an alternative. Disclosure alone does not establish that the recommendation serves the client.

lessons.title: Technology and judgment
lessons.body: Automation can reduce repetitive work and expand access, but it also creates data, security and model risks. A polished output is not evidence of correctness. Specify who owns a decision, which inputs are reliable, and where review is required.
lessons.example: A summary reads convincingly but cites last year’s terms. Check source version and effective date before relying on it.

lessons.title: From savings to useful investment
lessons.body: Financial services help households and institutions move purchasing power across time and manage uncertainty. Financing can support equipment, research or infrastructure, but the mere existence of a financial product does not prove social benefit. Good capital allocation requires information, credible claims and accountable decision makers. Intermediation can reduce search costs while adding fees and agency problems.
lessons.example: A manufacturer issues bonds to finance new machinery. Investors receive a contractual claim, not ownership of the machinery itself unless collateral terms provide it.

lessons.title: Buy side, sell side and service providers
lessons.body: Buy-side organizations manage assets for clients or themselves. Sell-side firms often facilitate issuance, research and transactions. These labels describe activities rather than airtight organizational boundaries. Custody, administration, recordkeeping and technology support both sides. An investment bank can have asset-management affiliates, so map the specific function and legal entity instead of relying on the parent company label.
lessons.example: A pension fund hires an investment manager, trades through a broker and uses a custodian. Each has a different role in the same investment journey.

lessons.title: Governance and the control environment
lessons.body: A board oversees the organization; management runs it. Effective governance makes decision rights, accountability and escalation clear. Controls can prevent mistakes, detect them or support recovery. Segregating incompatible responsibilities reduces opportunities for concealment, but no single control is perfect. Evidence that a review occurred should identify what was checked, by whom and when, rather than merely displaying a completed checkbox.
lessons.example: A person initiating a payment should not also be its sole approver and reconciler. A second review can challenge the amount, destination and authorization.

lessons.title: Services begin with a need
lessons.body: Financial planning connects resources to goals across saving, investment, protection, spending and estate considerations. An investment product is only one tool in that plan. Institutional clients may have liabilities, regulatory constraints or spending policies unlike a household’s. The first useful question is what the client needs to accomplish, not which product has the strongest recent return.
lessons.example: A foundation needs annual spending support while preserving long-term purchasing power. It cannot judge its portfolio only by one month’s return.

lessons.title: Ethical decisions under deadline pressure
lessons.body: Pressure does not remove professional responsibility. Separate facts from assumptions, identify duties and stakeholders, evaluate alternatives, act and reflect. A gift, performance target or personal holding may influence judgment without an obvious instruction to act improperly. Ethical escalation is more effective when it explains the concern and a workable alternative rather than merely saying no.
lessons.example: A launch deadline approaches, but the reviewed disclosure no longer matches the product terms. Escalate the discrepancy and the release options rather than quietly publishing.

lessons.title: Regulation, disclosure and financial technology
lessons.body: Regulation may address products, participants, conduct, disclosure and system stability. Requirements differ by activity and jurisdiction. Disclosure helps investors evaluate an offering but does not mean a regulator endorses it. FinTech can improve delivery, matching and analysis while changing cyber, privacy and operational exposures. Use cases need both an intended benefit and a control plan.
lessons.example: A digital advice tool can scale a questionnaire. It still needs accurate inputs, appropriate methodology, clear limitations and oversight.

modules.title: Markets, orders and vehicles
modules.summary: Separate the asset from its trading venue, investment vehicle and account wrapper.
objectives: Explain mutual funds, ETFs and managed accounts

lessons.title: Issuance versus trading
lessons.body: In a primary-market transaction the issuer raises capital. In a secondary-market transaction an existing security changes hands. A liquid secondary market can make investors more willing to participate in primary issuance.
lessons.example: A company sells new shares in an offering; later, one investor sells those shares to another on an exchange. Only the first transaction directly raises money for the issuer.

lessons.title: Price is not the whole cost
lessons.body: A buyer normally pays the ask and a seller receives the bid. Their gap is the spread. Commissions, price impact and delay also matter. A market order prioritizes execution, not a guaranteed price. A limit order controls the acceptable price but may never execute.
lessons.example: At a $9.90 bid and $10.10 ask, an immediate buyer generally pays $10.10, before other charges.

lessons.title: Vehicles are containers
lessons.body: A mutual fund or ETF pools investments. A managed account holds a client-specific portfolio. A fund of funds owns other funds. An account such as an IRA is a legal/tax wrapper, not an asset class. A stock fund inside a Roth IRA is still exposed to stock-market risk.
lessons.example: A Roth IRA can hold a stock fund or bond fund. The wrapper does not tell you the underlying investment risk.

lessons.title: Mechanics and innovation
lessons.body: Clearing establishes obligations and settlement exchanges assets and payment. DeFi can automate financial transactions using distributed networks and smart contracts, but it does not remove code, liquidity, governance or fraud risk.
lessons.example: A trade has the correct price but an incorrect destination account. It can still fail to settle.

lessons.title: Issuance, underwriting and corporate financing
lessons.body: An initial public offering introduces shares to public investors; later offerings can raise additional capital. A rights offering gives existing owners specified purchase rights. Debt issuance and equity issuance create different claims and can change financing risk or ownership percentages. Underwriters and advisers support transactions, but the offering documents remain essential for understanding the actual terms.
lessons.example: A company with 100 shares issues 25 more. A holder of 10 shares who buys none moves from 10% ownership to 8%, before considering other changes.

lessons.title: Trading venues and market structure
lessons.body: Order-driven venues bring buy and sell instructions together; quote-driven markets rely on dealer quotations. A broker commonly acts for a client, while a dealer may trade as principal. Transparency, competition, liquidity and available order types affect execution. A familiar exchange name is not sufficient to judge whether a particular instrument will trade easily in stressed conditions.
lessons.example: A dealer offers to buy a bond at 98 and sell it at 99. The investor buying immediately pays 99 before other applicable charges.

lessons.title: Orders, positions and execution tradeoffs
lessons.body: A long position usually benefits from a rising asset price. A short sale involves selling borrowed securities and later returning equivalent securities, creating borrowing and potentially very large loss risks. Order conditions exchange one kind of certainty for another: limit prices do not guarantee execution. Trading costs include visible charges and less visible spread, market impact and opportunity costs.
lessons.example: An investor buys 20 shares at $40 and later sells at $42. Before costs and income, the gain is $40, or 5% of the initial $800.

lessons.title: From trade to settlement
lessons.body: Trade capture, confirmation, clearing and settlement are separate steps. Failures can arise from mismatched instructions, missing assets, insufficient cash or incorrect account details. Settlement conventions vary by instrument and market; do not assume one global cycle. Reconciliation compares independent records and helps reveal discrepancies that can affect positions, cash and client reporting.
lessons.example: Two systems agree on the security and quantity but disagree on the settlement account. The economics may match while the payment delivery still fails.

lessons.title: Fund structure, NAV and investor experience
lessons.body: A fund’s NAV per share is its net assets divided by shares outstanding. An ETF’s exchange price can differ from NAV. Mutual-fund purchase and redemption processing follows its valuation and order rules. Index funds can use full replication, sampling or other permitted techniques, so expenses and implementation can cause performance to diverge from the index. Vehicle choice does not alone determine asset risk.
lessons.example: A fund has $10 million in assets, $1 million in liabilities and 900,000 shares. Net assets are $9 million and NAV is $10 per share.

lessons.title: Pooled alternatives and tailored accounts
lessons.body: A hedge fund, fund of funds and managed account describe different ways to access strategies. Redemption restrictions, fee layers, transparency and client control can differ. A fund of funds offers manager selection but may introduce additional expenses. A managed account can tailor holdings, yet customization depends on its mandate and platform. DeFi changes the operating arrangement rather than making these economic questions disappear.
lessons.example: A fund of funds charges its own fee while underlying funds also incur expenses. The investor should evaluate the combined cost, not only the top-level charge.

modules.title: Investment instruments and quantitative tools
modules.summary: Understand cash flows, claims, valuation and the risks attached to each instrument.
objectives: Compare equity, debt, derivatives and alternatives

lessons.title: Time changes value
lessons.body: For a constant annual rate r over n years, future value is PV × (1+r)^n. Present value reverses that calculation. Net present value discounts future cash flows and subtracts initial cost. These calculations depend on assumptions, not promises.
lessons.example: $100 at 10% for two years becomes $121, because the second year also earns on the first year’s interest.

lessons.title: Ownership versus lending
lessons.body: Common shares are residual ownership claims; dividends are not guaranteed. Bonds are contractual debt claims, subject to issuer default and terms. For otherwise similar fixed-rate bonds, rising required yields reduce prices. Longer duration generally means greater sensitivity to yield changes.
lessons.example: A company’s shares fall and its bond credit spread widens after a weak earnings report. Equity and debt can both lose value for different reasons.

lessons.title: Derivatives and alternatives
lessons.body: A forward or future creates obligations linked to an underlying item. An option buyer acquires a right, while the seller takes an obligation. Swaps exchange cash-flow patterns. Private equity, property and commodities have distinct return drivers, valuation challenges and liquidity constraints.
lessons.example: An importer hedges a future foreign-currency payment but still faces supplier and timing risks.

lessons.title: Measure the uncertainty
lessons.body: The mean summarizes an average, the median identifies the middle observation and standard deviation measures dispersion around the mean. Correlation measures linear co-movement, not causation. Real returns can have extreme outcomes that a normal model understates.
lessons.example: Two investments had low historical correlation. That is useful evidence, not a promise their future losses will never coincide.

lessons.title: Compounding, discounting and project value
lessons.body: Discounted cash-flow analysis requires a timeline, cash-flow amounts and a rate consistent with their risk and units. Discount each cash flow separately. Net present value adds these discounted amounts and subtracts the initial cost. A positive calculated NPV depends on the assumptions being credible; it is not a promise. Keep annual versus monthly rates and nominal versus real values consistent.
lessons.example: Pay $95 today for $110 in one year. At a 10% required return the future payment is worth $100 today, so NPV is $5.

lessons.title: Statistics without false confidence
lessons.body: Averages can conceal unstable or skewed outcomes. The median is less affected by a single extreme value than the arithmetic mean. Volatility summarizes dispersion but does not capture every risk. Correlations estimated in one period may change during stress. A normal distribution can be a useful model, but assuming it fits every asset can understate unusual losses and asymmetry.
lessons.example: Returns of 2%, 3% and 25% have a 10% arithmetic mean but a 3% median. The unusually large result pulls the mean upward.

lessons.title: Equity valuation and corporate actions
lessons.body: Equity valuation connects expected future benefits with risk and price. Dividend-based models require assumptions about distributions and growth, while multiples compare prices with metrics such as earnings. Neither replaces understanding the business. Corporate actions can change units, claims or cash distributions. A split is not by itself new wealth; buybacks, issuance and dividends require examining financing, price and consequences.
lessons.example: A $60 share with $3 earnings per share trades at 20 times earnings. That multiple alone does not show whether the share is cheap relative to its risks and growth.

lessons.title: Debt cash flows, ranking and embedded choices
lessons.body: Bond analysis begins with promised payments and the conditions that can alter them. Seniority affects claim priority; collateral may support recovery but is not a guarantee. A call favors issuer flexibility, often when refinancing becomes attractive, while a put can give the holder an exit right under specified terms. Yield comparisons require consistent maturity, credit, optionality, currency and tax treatment.
lessons.example: An issuer can call a bond at 100 after rates fall. A holder expecting a high coupon for many years may instead have to reinvest the returned principal at lower yields.

lessons.title: Derivative payoffs and hedging choices
lessons.body: Derivatives transfer exposure rather than creating certainty. Futures typically require margin and daily settlement; forwards are often customized bilateral arrangements. A purchased option has an upfront premium and may expire unused. A swap can exchange fixed and floating payments. A hedge should match the relevant exposure, horizon and size; imperfect matching creates basis risk and can leave liquidity needs.
lessons.example: Buy a call with strike $50 for a $3 premium. At expiration with the share at $58, intrinsic value is $8 and profit before costs is $5 per share.

lessons.title: Alternatives, illiquidity and valuation
lessons.body: Alternative investments may provide distinct exposures but often require additional due diligence. Private valuations can update less frequently than public prices, so reported smoothness is not proof of low economic risk. Property brings tenant, maintenance and financing risks. Commodity exposures can depend on storage or futures-curve behavior. Diversification benefits must be weighed against fees, complexity, concentration and exit constraints.
lessons.example: A private fund reports quarterly values while public stocks reprice each day. Comparing volatility without considering appraisal timing can create a misleading impression of stability.

modules.title: Economics and financial statements
modules.summary: Connect economic forces and company reports to investment decisions.
objectives: Explain supply, demand and economic cycles
Read the three main statements together

lessons.title: Microeconomics
lessons.body: Demand describes willingness and ability to buy at different prices; supply describes willingness and ability to sell. Their interaction helps determine prices. Elasticity measures responsiveness. A profitable firm still needs to consider competition, cost structure and customer substitution.
lessons.example: An increase in input costs can reduce supply even if consumer tastes have not changed.

lessons.title: Macroeconomics
lessons.body: GDP measures production, not personal well-being. Inflation reduces purchasing power. Central banks use monetary tools while governments use spending and taxation as fiscal policy. Policy changes affect growth, financing costs and exchange rates with uncertain timing.
lessons.example: A central-bank rate change and a government infrastructure budget are different policy tools with different transmission paths.

lessons.title: Trade and currencies
lessons.body: Comparative advantage concerns lower opportunity cost, not absolute output. Exchange-rate movements affect translated investment returns and the competitiveness of importers and exporters. A currency hedge changes exposures but has costs and does not eliminate every risk.
lessons.example: An overseas investment rises 5% locally but its currency falls against the investor’s home currency; the translated return can be lower.

lessons.title: Three perspectives on a business
lessons.body: The balance sheet is a point-in-time view of assets, liabilities and equity. The income statement reports revenue and expenses over a period. Cash flow separates operating, investing and financing activity. Profit and cash are different because recognition and payment dates differ.
lessons.example: A business records a credit sale today but collects the customer’s payment next month, so earnings and cash timing differ.

lessons.title: Demand, elasticity and market equilibrium
lessons.body: Separate a movement along a demand curve caused by the good’s price from a shift caused by income, preferences or substitutes. Supply can shift with input costs or technology. Elasticity describes proportional responsiveness; a simple estimate divides percentage quantity change by percentage price change. Competitive equilibrium is a model, not a claim that real markets always adjust instantly.
lessons.example: A 10% price rise is associated with a 20% decline in quantity demanded. The simple elasticity estimate is −2, indicating an elastic response in magnitude.

lessons.title: Costs, profit and competitive settings
lessons.body: Total profit is revenue less total cost. Fixed costs do not vary with short-run output in the model; variable costs do. Marginal analysis asks what changes when one additional unit is produced or sold. Competitive structure influences pricing power, but barriers and substitution can evolve. Accounting profit and economic profit differ because economic analysis includes opportunity costs of resources.
lessons.example: At 100 units sold for $12 each, revenue is $1,200. If total cost is $950, accounting profit is $250 before any omitted items.

lessons.title: Growth, inflation and policy transmission
lessons.body: Economic growth can come from more resources or better productivity. Business cycles describe fluctuations around longer-term activity, with indicators offering imperfect clues. Nominal growth includes price effects; real growth adjusts for them. Monetary and fiscal decisions influence incentives and demand, but time lags, expectations and supply conditions affect results. No single policy announcement determines every asset price.
lessons.example: An investment earns 6% while prices rise 4%. Its exact real return is 1.06/1.04 − 1, about 1.92%, not 6%.

lessons.title: Trade, external accounts and exchange rates
lessons.body: Trade can benefit parties with different opportunity costs even when one is more productive at everything. The balance of payments records cross-border transactions under accounting conventions. Currency regimes range from floating to various managed or fixed arrangements. Foreign-exchange returns depend on the quote direction: always specify which currency buys which. Hedging can reduce a chosen currency exposure while adding costs and counterparties.
lessons.example: An asset worth €1,000 converts to $1,100 at $1.10 per euro. At $1.00 per euro, it converts to $1,000 even if the asset’s euro price is unchanged.

lessons.title: Connect the financial statements
lessons.body: Statements are linked, so analyze transactions across them. Borrowing cash raises assets and liabilities but is not revenue. A credit sale can raise earnings and receivables before cash arrives. Depreciation reduces accounting earnings without a current cash payment, although buying the asset used cash earlier. Retained earnings connect accumulated results and distributions to equity, subject to other accounting changes.
lessons.example: Borrow $500 in cash. Assets rise $500 and liabilities rise $500. The borrowing is financing cash flow, not $500 of operating revenue.

lessons.title: Ratios, comparability and warning signs
lessons.body: Ratios turn statements into questions rather than automatic decisions. A current ratio compares current assets with current liabilities; a margin relates profit to revenue. Leverage ratios examine debt financing. Compare similar businesses and consistent definitions, inspect trends, and read footnotes. One unusually strong ratio can result from timing, accounting policy or a denominator that has become very small.
lessons.example: Current assets of $240 and current liabilities of $120 give a current ratio of 2. That does not prove all assets are readily convertible to cash.

modules.title: Client needs, portfolios and performance
modules.summary: Start with the investor, then assess the portfolio and its results.
objectives: Translate goals into an investment policy
Evaluate returns, benchmarks and operational risk

lessons.title: Define success first
lessons.body: An investment policy statement connects objectives to constraints such as time horizon, liquidity, taxes and legal requirements. Risk willingness is emotional comfort; risk capacity is financial ability to bear losses. They can differ sharply.
lessons.example: Someone may feel comfortable taking risk but need the entire investment for tuition in six months, limiting financial risk capacity.

lessons.title: Build a portfolio, not a collection
lessons.body: Asset allocation sets the mix of exposures. Diversification across genuinely different holdings can reduce concentration risk but cannot prevent all losses. Rebalancing restores a chosen mix and can create costs or taxes. Two funds with similar holdings may add little diversification.
lessons.example: Two different funds can both hold the same large technology companies, leaving substantial overlapping exposure.

lessons.title: Judge performance fairly
lessons.body: Total return combines price change and income. Time-weighted return reduces the effect of external cash-flow timing; money-weighted return reflects the investor cash-flow experience. Compare a strategy with a relevant benchmark, similar risk and consistent fee treatment.
lessons.example: Compare two funds over the same dates and currency, and establish whether reported returns include fees.

lessons.title: Risk and attribution
lessons.body: Tracking error measures variation in active returns; alpha estimates performance beyond a specified model and is model dependent. Attribution separates sources such as allocation and selection. Value at Risk is a modeled loss threshold at a stated confidence and horizon, not a maximum possible loss. Operational and compliance failures can harm investors even when markets are calm.
lessons.example: A one-day VaR estimate does not say what the largest possible loss is during a crisis.

lessons.title: Investor objectives and constraints
lessons.body: Individual and institutional investors can pursue growth, income, capital preservation or liability funding, often in combination. Specify what success means in real terms, when cash is needed and which constraints apply. Willingness to take risk is not the same as capacity. A change in family circumstances, funding status or regulation can justify revisiting an investment policy without reacting to every market headline.
lessons.example: A client loves speculative investments but needs the money for a house deposit in six months. Enthusiasm does not increase the financial ability to absorb a large loss.

lessons.title: Diversification and portfolio construction
lessons.body: Portfolio risk depends on position sizes and how exposures interact. Many holdings can still share one economic driver. Strategic allocation establishes a longer-term mix, while tactical choices depart from that mix for specific reasons. Rebalancing disciplines drift but can involve transaction costs and tax consequences. A portfolio should be evaluated as a whole, not by whether every position individually outperforms.
lessons.example: A 60/40 stock/bond portfolio grows to 70/30 after stocks rally. Restoring 60/40 generally requires reducing stocks or directing new money toward bonds.

lessons.title: Active choices, passive choices and inefficiency
lessons.body: An active strategy makes deliberate departures from a benchmark or other reference to pursue its objective. A passive strategy seeks a specified exposure, often at lower implementation cost, but its chosen index still embeds rules and concentration. Market inefficiencies may create opportunities, yet identifying and exploiting them after costs is difficult. Evaluate process, capacity, costs and mandate rather than assuming one label guarantees success.
lessons.example: A broad index can become concentrated when a few constituents grow very large. Passive implementation does not mean the resulting portfolio has no concentration risk.

lessons.title: A practical risk-management cycle
lessons.body: Identify exposures, assess their significance, choose responses, implement controls and monitor results. Risk responses may include avoiding, reducing, transferring or accepting an exposure. A risk register needs an owner and trigger for action, not just a severity color. Investment risks interact with operational and compliance risks, so good controls consider the full path from decision to execution and reporting.
lessons.example: A fund-change team identifies a stale identifier feed. It assigns an owner, validates the replacement and monitors downstream records after launch.

lessons.title: Performance calculations and suitable benchmarks
lessons.body: Return calculations must specify the period, income, costs and cash flows. Chain-linked time-weighted returns use multiplication, not simply adding period percentages. A relevant benchmark should match the opportunity set and be defined before evaluation rather than selected after seeing results. Absolute return shows what happened; relative return asks how it compares with a suitable reference.
lessons.example: A portfolio gains 10% then loses 10%. $100 becomes $110 then $99, so the cumulative return is −1%, not zero.

lessons.title: Risk-adjusted results, attribution and model limits
lessons.body: Risk-adjusted measures summarize a particular risk model, not total investment quality. The Sharpe ratio uses excess return and total volatility; other measures use different denominators. Attribution can separate allocation and selection effects under a stated methodology. Alpha depends on its model and data. VaR has a confidence level and horizon; scenarios and stress testing explore what a single threshold can miss.
lessons.example: A portfolio earns 8%, a risk-free reference is 2% and volatility is 12%. Its simple Sharpe ratio is (8−2)/12 = 0.5 for consistently measured inputs.

questions.question: What is a custodian primarily responsible for?
questions.explanation: Custody concerns safekeeping and administration, not guaranteed returns or portfolio management.

questions.question: Which situation most clearly creates a conflict of interest?
options: A bond pays its scheduled coupon
A manager receives compensation for favoring a product
questions.explanation: Compensation tied to a recommendation can pull incentives away from client interests.

questions.question: A legally permitted disclosure is technically accurate but likely to mislead. What is the best next step?
questions.explanation: Ethical judgment includes clarity and fairness beyond minimum legality.

questions.question: Who normally seeks capital by selling a new security?
options: A transfer agent acting only as recordkeeper
questions.explanation: Issuers use securities offerings to obtain financing.

questions.question: Which task belongs most closely to investment operations?
questions.explanation: Operations helps ensure transaction and position records agree.

questions.question: Why does a product change need downstream dependency review?
options: It removes the need for owners
Multiple systems and disclosures may rely on the changed field
questions.explanation: A small upstream change can have consequences across systems and communications.

questions.question: What is the strongest control for an automated financial summary?
options: Trace inputs and require appropriate review
questions.explanation: Traceability and review address errors that polished prose can conceal.

questions.question: What should happen to a material conflict after disclosure?
options: It must still be appropriately managed
questions.explanation: Disclosure is a step, not a substitute for managing the conflict.

questions.question: Which is an investment information service?
questions.explanation: Information providers support decisions with research or data.

questions.question: What is a key economic function of investment markets?
questions.explanation: Markets connect those with capital to those seeking to use it.

questions.question: A colleague gives you confidential client data unrelated to your task. What is prudent?
options: Treat access as permission for all uses
Follow access controls and avoid unnecessary use
Upload it to any public tool
questions.explanation: Access does not justify uses outside authorized purpose.

questions.question: Which statement about regulation is most accurate?
options: Rules aim to address market conduct and investor protection
Rules guarantee each investment is safe
questions.explanation: Oversight does not eliminate investment risk.

questions.question: Who receives proceeds when an investor buys an existing share from another investor?
questions.explanation: Secondary trading transfers ownership between investors rather than directly financing the issuer.

questions.question: A quote is 24.90 bid and 25.10 ask. What is the spread?
questions.explanation: Ask minus bid is 25.10 − 24.90 = 0.20.

questions.question: Which order prioritizes execution over a specified price?
questions.explanation: A market order seeks available execution but the price can change.

questions.question: A buy limit order is placed at $30. Which execution is consistent with its price condition?
options: Any price if the market rises
questions.explanation: A buy limit specifies the highest acceptable execution price.

questions.question: What is an ETF?
options: A pooled fund whose shares trade on an exchange
questions.explanation: ETF describes a vehicle and trading structure, not necessarily passive management.

questions.question: What distinguishes a mutual fund share class?
options: It always owns a completely different portfolio
It is a separate asset class
Fees and eligibility may differ while sharing the portfolio
questions.explanation: Classes commonly share underlying holdings but have different expenses or access rules.

questions.question: An IRA holding a stock fund is best described as what?
options: An account wrapper holding an investment vehicle
questions.explanation: Account wrapper, vehicle and underlying asset are separate layers.

questions.question: What happens at settlement?
options: Securities and payment are exchanged under trade obligations
questions.explanation: Settlement fulfills the exchange established by the trade.

questions.question: What does a fund of funds primarily hold?
questions.explanation: A fund of funds obtains exposure through underlying funds.

questions.question: Why might an ETF market price differ from NAV?
options: Trading supply and demand can create a premium or discount
questions.explanation: Market price and calculated net asset value are different measures.

questions.question: What is a key smart-contract risk?
questions.explanation: Code can fail or be exploited; automation does not remove risk.

questions.question: A client owns securities directly in a tailored portfolio. What structure fits?
options: A single mandatory pooled share class
questions.explanation: A managed account can hold a client-specific portfolio directly.

questions.question: What is $1,000 compounded at 5% for two years?
What is the present value of $1,100 received in one year at a 10% discount rate?
questions.explanation: Discount the future cash flow: $1,100 ÷ (1 + 0.10) = $1,000 today. Discounting reverses compounding; it does not subtract 10% of the future value.

questions.question: For an otherwise unchanged fixed-rate bond, what generally happens when required yields rise?
questions.explanation: Existing fixed cash flows become less valuable when discounted at a higher rate.

questions.question: What is common equity's claim in liquidation?
questions.explanation: Common shareholders bear residual risk after creditors and senior claims.

questions.question: Which option gives its buyer the right to buy an underlying asset?
questions.explanation: A call grants a purchase right under specified terms.

questions.question: Which option gives its buyer the right to sell an underlying asset?
questions.explanation: A put grants a sale right under specified terms.

questions.question: Which statistic measures dispersion around the mean?
questions.explanation: Standard deviation summarizes variation, not the center alone.

questions.question: A correlation of zero implies what?
options: No linear relationship in the measured sample
questions.explanation: Nonlinear relationships and changing conditions may still exist.

questions.question: What is a major private-equity investment constraint?
options: Limited liquidity and uncertain exit timing
questions.explanation: Private assets may be difficult to sell and lack observable market prices.

questions.question: What does a stock split ordinarily change directly?
options: The firm's total economic value automatically
questions.explanation: A split changes units, not enterprise value by itself.

questions.question: Which risk concerns an issuer failing to pay?
questions.explanation: Credit risk is the possibility of failure to meet debt obligations.

questions.question: Two bonds are otherwise similar. Which generally has more yield sensitivity?
options: The one with a shorter name
The one held in an IRA
questions.explanation: Duration approximates price sensitivity to yield changes.

questions.question: Which statement is a snapshot at a point in time?
questions.explanation: Assets, liabilities and equity are measured at the reporting date.

questions.question: What is the accounting identity?
questions.explanation: The balance sheet links resources to creditors' and owners' claims.

questions.question: Which activity is usually a financing cash flow?
questions.explanation: Raising or repaying capital is financing activity.

questions.question: Why can profit differ from cash generated?
options: Accrual recognition and payment timing differ
questions.explanation: Credit sales, depreciation and working-capital changes separate earnings from cash.

questions.question: What does inflation describe?
options: A sustained increase in the general price level
A guaranteed rise in real wages
questions.explanation: Inflation is an aggregate price phenomenon, not uniform changes in every item.

questions.question: Which is fiscal policy?
questions.explanation: Fiscal policy is a government budget tool.

questions.question: Which is monetary policy?
options: Central-bank actions influencing money and financing conditions
questions.explanation: Monetary policy operates through central-bank tools.

questions.question: Demand increases while supply is unchanged. What is the basic competitive-market expectation?
options: A higher equilibrium price and quantity
questions.explanation: A rightward demand shift raises equilibrium price and quantity in the basic model.

questions.question: What does comparative advantage depend on?
questions.explanation: Trade gains can exist when parties face different opportunity costs.

questions.question: A US investor's foreign asset is unchanged in local price, but its currency weakens against USD. What happens to its USD value before hedging?
questions.explanation: The same local-currency amount converts into fewer dollars.

questions.question: What does price elasticity of demand measure?
options: Quantity demanded's responsiveness to price changes
questions.explanation: Elasticity compares proportional changes in quantity and price.

questions.question: Which statement about GDP is best?
options: It measures production within an economy over a period
It is identical to stock-market value
questions.explanation: GDP is an output measure, not a complete welfare measure.

questions.question: Risk capacity means what?
questions.explanation: Capacity depends on circumstances such as resources and time horizon.

questions.question: What does an investment policy statement do?
options: Documents objectives and constraints guiding decisions
questions.explanation: An IPS provides a decision framework rather than a performance promise.

questions.question: What does diversification not guarantee?
questions.explanation: Market-wide losses can affect a diversified portfolio.

questions.question: What is rebalancing?
options: Adjusting holdings toward the intended allocation
Always buying the best recent performer
questions.explanation: Rebalancing restores portfolio weights and may involve costs or taxes.

questions.question: A portfolio rises from $100 to $106 and pays $2 income. Ignoring fees, what is its total return?
questions.explanation: Price gain plus income is 8 on a starting value of 100.

questions.question: Which return measure removes the impact of external cash-flow timing through subperiod linking?
questions.explanation: Time weighting helps evaluate the investment process apart from investor contribution timing.

questions.question: Which return measure is sensitive to contribution and withdrawal timing?
questions.explanation: Money-weighted return reflects amounts and timing of investor cash flows.

questions.question: What makes a benchmark useful?
options: It reflects the portfolio's intended opportunity set and risk
It is whichever index performed worst
It always has the highest return
questions.explanation: An appropriate benchmark supports meaningful comparison.

questions.question: Tracking error measures what?
options: Variation in returns relative to a benchmark
questions.explanation: Tracking error is the standard deviation of active returns.

questions.question: What is a limitation of Value at Risk?
options: It is the maximum possible loss
Losses can exceed the stated threshold
questions.explanation: VaR is conditional on a model, horizon and confidence level.

questions.question: A trade fails because a file was mapped incorrectly. Which risk is most directly illustrated?
questions.explanation: Process and system failures are operational risks.

questions.question: What should a fair fund-performance comparison align?
options: Period, fees, currency and relevant risk
questions.explanation: Inconsistent bases can make performance comparisons misleading.

questions.question: A company sells a new bond to finance equipment. What happens economically?
options: The investor becomes the chief executive
questions.explanation: New debt financing links investor capital to the issuer’s funding needs.

questions.question: Why can an intermediary help a small investor?
options: It can lower search and transaction burdens
questions.explanation: Intermediaries provide services and scale, but costs and conflicts still require evaluation.

questions.question: A new investment product collects large fees but poorly serves its target clients. Which conclusion is most reasonable?
options: A high fee proves high quality
Product innovation alone is not proof of client benefit
questions.explanation: Assess the product’s actual function and client outcomes rather than its novelty.

questions.question: A pension portfolio manager selects securities for beneficiaries. Which function is this?
questions.explanation: The manager makes investment decisions for assets on behalf of clients.

questions.question: A firm underwrites a corporate bond offering. Which activity is illustrated?
questions.explanation: Underwriting facilitates securities issuance; it does not eliminate issuer risk.

questions.question: Why identify the specific entity in a large financial group?
options: The parent name determines every duty
Different entities and roles can have different duties
questions.explanation: Organizational labels do not replace checking the actual service and applicable obligations.

questions.question: Which arrangement best separates incompatible payment responsibilities?
options: Different people initiate and independently approve
One person initiates approves and conceals the record
questions.explanation: Separation can reduce the risk that an error or misuse passes undetected.

questions.question: A reconciliation finds an already-posted error. What type of control is it primarily?
questions.explanation: A reconciliation identifies discrepancies after or during processing.

questions.question: What is the most useful approval evidence?
options: The reviewed version, reviewer, time and decision
questions.explanation: Traceable evidence supports accountability and later investigation.

questions.question: A client needs tuition money next month. Which input is especially important?
questions.explanation: A short horizon and spending need constrain suitable exposures.

questions.question: A pension fund evaluates investments against future benefit payments. What is central?
options: The number of apps it uses
questions.explanation: Institutional objectives often depend on liabilities to beneficiaries.

questions.question: What should ordinarily precede choosing an investment product?
questions.explanation: A product should serve a defined need within applicable constraints.

questions.question: A deadline conflicts with a known disclosure error. What is the best response?
options: Escalate the mismatch and propose a safe path
questions.explanation: Known inaccuracies need resolution through accountable decision making.

questions.question: A vendor offers a costly personal gift during selection. What should you do?
options: Treat the gift as proof of quality
Apply the firm’s gift/conflict rules and seek guidance
questions.explanation: The gift may impair impartiality or create the appearance of a conflict.

questions.question: After an ethical decision, why review the outcome?
options: To improve future judgment and controls
questions.explanation: Reflection can reveal overlooked harms, assumptions and process weaknesses.

questions.question: A fund is registered with a regulator. What follows?
options: Registration is not a guarantee of merit or safety
questions.explanation: Registration and disclosure requirements do not certify investment quality.

questions.question: A tool is accurate on test data but receives changed live inputs. What risk increases?
questions.explanation: Testing does not establish correctness under all future data conditions.

questions.question: Which FinTech rollout plan is strongest?
options: Define purpose, data access, testing and accountable review
questions.explanation: Useful automation needs governance as well as a compelling feature.

questions.question: A company has 100 shares and issues 25 new shares. An investor keeps 10 shares. What is the new ownership percentage?
questions.explanation: 10 divided by 125 equals 8%.

questions.question: Which transaction directly raises equity capital for an issuer?
questions.explanation: New issuance can deliver capital to the company.

questions.question: Why read an offering document even with an underwriter involved?
options: The security’s risks and terms still require evaluation
questions.explanation: Intermediary involvement does not eliminate the need to examine terms.

questions.question: A dealer quotes 98 bid and 99 ask. An immediate buyer generally transacts at which quoted side?
questions.explanation: The ask is the quoted selling price, subject to available size and conditions.

questions.question: What distinguishes principal dealing from agency brokerage?
options: The broker always issues the security
The dealer can trade for its own account
The dealer never bears inventory risk
questions.explanation: Principal dealing involves the firm’s own position rather than only acting for a client.

questions.question: A security trades infrequently on a recognized venue. What should you avoid assuming?
options: That listing guarantees easy exit at a stable price
questions.explanation: Liquidity depends on trading conditions and depth, not merely the venue.

questions.question: Buy 20 shares at $40 and sell at $42, ignoring costs and income. What is the gain?
questions.explanation: Each share gains $2. Multiply by 20 shares: 20 × ($42 − $40) = $40. The $840 selling proceeds include the original $800 investment, so proceeds are not the same as profit.

questions.question: A short position rises sharply in price. What happens absent an offset?
options: The position automatically becomes a bond
questions.explanation: Buying back at a higher price creates a loss, potentially beyond the initial proceeds.

questions.question: A buy limit remains below the market all day. What can happen?
questions.explanation: The acceptable price condition may never be met.

questions.question: Two systems show identical trade amounts but different settlement accounts. What is the concern?
options: Delivery can fail despite matching economics
There is no problem if price matches
questions.explanation: Correct settlement instructions matter independently of price and quantity.

questions.question: Why reconcile independent position records?
options: To detect missing or inconsistent transactions
questions.explanation: Independent records can reveal breaks not apparent in one system.

questions.question: How should a cross-border team determine settlement timing?
options: Assume every security settles the same day
Copy a rule from an unrelated asset
Check the instrument and applicable market rules
questions.explanation: Conventions differ and can change, requiring current authoritative verification.

questions.question: Assets are $10m, liabilities $1m and shares 900,000. What is NAV per share?
questions.explanation: Net assets of $9m divided by 900,000 shares equals $10.

questions.question: An ETF trades at $50.50 with a $50 NAV. What is its premium to NAV?
questions.explanation: (50.50 − 50) divided by 50 equals 1%.

questions.question: Why might an index fund trail its index?
options: An index is guaranteed while the fund is not
All index funds must be leveraged
questions.explanation: Costs and imperfect replication can produce tracking differences.

questions.question: What cost issue deserves attention in a fund of funds?
questions.explanation: Layered structures can introduce layered expenses.

questions.question: A client wants specific restricted securities excluded. Which may permit direct tailoring?
options: A separately managed account, subject to its mandate
questions.explanation: An SMA can allow client-specific holdings but platform and mandate limits still apply.

questions.question: A DeFi protocol has audited code. What remains necessary?
options: Treating audit as a government guarantee
Evaluation of economic, governance and operational risks
questions.explanation: Code review does not eliminate economic or governance failures.

questions.question: Pay $95 now for $110 in one year, discounting at 10%. What is NPV?
questions.explanation: Present value is 110/1.10 = 100; subtract 95 to get 5.

questions.question: Why should a model align cash-flow frequency and discount-rate units?
questions.explanation: Annual rates cannot be used as monthly rates without an appropriate conversion.

questions.question: If required return increases while positive future cash flows stay fixed, what happens to present value?
questions.explanation: Larger discount factors reduce the present value of future receipts.

questions.question: For returns 2%, 3% and 25%, what is the arithmetic mean?
For returns 2%, 3% and 25%, what is the median?
questions.explanation: The middle sorted observation is 3%.

questions.question: An estimated correlation was low in calm markets. What is prudent in stress planning?
questions.explanation: Relationships can shift when conditions change.

questions.question: A share costs $60 and earnings per share are $3. What is its P/E?
questions.explanation: 60 divided by 3 equals 20.

questions.question: A 2-for-1 split changes 10 shares priced at $80 into what, mechanically?
options: 20 shares at $80 each with guaranteed doubled wealth
questions.explanation: Units double and per-share value roughly halves, absent other changes.

questions.question: Two firms have the same P/E. What can still differ materially?
options: Their ratio must prove identical value
Their future returns are guaranteed equal
questions.explanation: A single multiple cannot capture the business and risk differences.

questions.question: Falling rates make an issuer’s call option more attractive. What may the holder face?
options: Automatic conversion to cash at twice par
Earlier redemption and reinvestment at lower yields
questions.explanation: A callable bond can shorten the investor’s expected income stream.

questions.question: In general, which claim has priority over common equity in liquidation?
options: Debt claims under applicable ranking rules
questions.explanation: Creditors generally rank ahead of residual common ownership.

questions.question: Why is comparing only two bonds’ headline yields insufficient?
options: Credit, maturity and option terms may differ
Yield has no relationship to price
questions.explanation: A higher yield may compensate for additional or different risks.

questions.question: A call costs $3, strike is $50, and final stock price is $58. What is profit per share before costs?
questions.explanation: Payoff is 58 − 50 = 8; subtract the 3 premium to get 5.

questions.question: A put with strike $40 expires with the stock at $45. What is its intrinsic value?
questions.explanation: Selling at 40 is inferior to the 45 market price, so intrinsic value is zero.

questions.question: A hedge uses a related but different commodity from the one a firm buys. What remains?
questions.explanation: The hedge and actual exposure may not move together.

questions.question: A private asset’s quarterly valuation looks smooth. What should you avoid concluding?
options: That it may require due diligence
That its economic risk is necessarily low
questions.explanation: Infrequent or appraisal-based marks can conceal interim changes.

questions.question: Which issue is specific to directly owned rental property?
options: A fixed public-market price at all times
questions.explanation: Property income depends partly on tenants and ongoing operating needs.

questions.question: Why might commodity-futures returns differ from spot-price changes?
options: Futures always equal physical ownership returns
Contract rolling and curve conditions affect returns
questions.explanation: Futures exposure includes contract mechanics beyond spot movement.

questions.question: Price rises 10% and quantity demanded falls 20%. What is the simple elasticity estimate?
questions.explanation: −20% divided by 10% equals −2.

questions.question: New technology lowers production costs, other things equal. Which change is most plausible?
questions.explanation: Lower costs can make suppliers willing to offer more at each price.

questions.question: Consumers favor a product more strongly at every price. What is this?
options: Only movement along an unchanged curve
questions.explanation: Changed preferences can alter demand independently of the good’s own price.

questions.question: 100 units sell for $12 and total cost is $950. What is profit?
questions.explanation: Revenue of 1200 less cost of 950 equals 250.

questions.question: What is marginal cost?
options: The additional cost of one more unit
questions.explanation: Marginal analysis focuses on incremental changes.

questions.question: Why can economic profit be lower than accounting profit?
options: It excludes alternative uses of capital
It is always equal to revenue
questions.explanation: Accounting may omit implicit costs included in economic analysis.

questions.question: Nominal return is 6% and inflation 4%. What is the approximate exact real return?
questions.explanation: 1.06 divided by 1.04 minus 1 is about 0.0192.

questions.question: What can increase output without increasing labor hours?
questions.explanation: Producing more per unit of input raises productivity.

questions.question: Why not assume a rate cut immediately produces a fixed growth increase?
options: Policy effects involve lags and changing conditions
questions.explanation: Transmission depends on borrowers, expectations, supply and other factors.

questions.question: €1,000 converts at $1.10 per euro. What is the dollar value?
questions.explanation: Multiply euros by dollars per euro.

questions.question: The quote changes from $1.10 to $1.00 per euro. What happened to the euro relative to the dollar?
options: The quote proves inflation is zero
questions.explanation: Each euro buys fewer dollars.

questions.question: Can mutually beneficial trade occur if one party is absolutely more productive at both goods?
options: Only if all costs are equal
Yes, if relative opportunity costs differ
questions.explanation: Comparative advantage depends on relative opportunity costs, not absolute productivity alone.

questions.question: A business borrows $500 cash. What is the immediate balance-sheet effect?
questions.explanation: Cash is an asset and the borrowing creates a liability.

questions.question: A credit sale is recognized but not collected. What can happen?
options: The sale becomes a loan from a bank
Revenue and receivables rise without immediate cash
questions.explanation: Accrual recognition can precede customer payment.

questions.question: Which statement about depreciation is correct?
options: It can reduce earnings without a current-period cash outflow
It always equals cash paid that day
It eliminates the asset’s original cost
questions.explanation: Depreciation allocates a previously incurred asset cost over periods.

questions.question: Current assets are $240 and current liabilities $120. What is the current ratio?
questions.explanation: 240 divided by 120 equals 2.

questions.question: Net income is $15 on revenue of $100. What is net profit margin?
questions.explanation: 15 divided by 100 equals 15%.

questions.question: A current ratio is high because inventory is obsolete. What is the lesson?
options: Asset quality matters alongside the ratio
questions.explanation: Reported totals need interpretation, including realizability of assets.

questions.question: A client enjoys risk but needs the money in six months. Which distinction matters?
options: Capacity is only a personality trait
questions.explanation: Financial constraints can limit prudent risk even when emotional willingness is high.

questions.question: A foundation must spend 4% annually. What should its policy address?
options: Spending, liquidity and long-term objectives together
questions.explanation: Spending obligations and sustainability must be considered jointly.

questions.question: Which event most clearly warrants reviewing an investment policy?
options: A material change in the client’s liquidity needs
questions.explanation: Policy review should respond to meaningful changes in objectives or constraints.

questions.question: A portfolio drifts from 60/40 to 70/30 stocks/bonds. Which action moves it toward target?
options: Buy more of every stock equally
Reduce stock weight or add proportionally more bonds
questions.explanation: Rebalancing restores weights; the implementation can use trades or cash flows.

questions.question: Ten funds all own similar technology stocks. What is the concern?
options: Underlying concentration despite many fund names
Automatic equal exposure to every sector
questions.explanation: Count exposures, not just product labels.

questions.question: Why consider tax and trading effects before rebalancing?
options: Taxes never depend on account type
questions.explanation: Restoring weights is a decision that still needs practical implementation review.

questions.question: An index fund becomes dominated by a few large firms. What is true?
options: Concentration only occurs in active funds
Passive investing can still have concentration risk
questions.explanation: Index construction and market movements determine exposures.

questions.question: A strategy earns 1% more gross return but costs 1.5% more, all else equal. What happens to relative net return?
questions.explanation: The additional fee exceeds the gross advantage by 0.5 percentage points.

questions.question: What should an active strategy’s evaluation include?
options: Process, risk, fees and fit with the mandate
questions.explanation: A systematic assessment avoids confusing luck or different risk with skill.

questions.question: A risk register lists a red risk with no owner or response. What is missing?
questions.explanation: Risk identification alone does not manage the exposure.

questions.question: Buying insurance for an insurable operational exposure primarily does what?
options: Transfers some financial consequences under policy terms
questions.explanation: Insurance can transfer specified losses but does not prevent all incidents.

questions.question: A new process control is implemented. What should follow?
options: Monitoring whether it works as intended
questions.explanation: Controls need evidence of ongoing effectiveness.

questions.question: A portfolio gains 10% then loses 10%. What is cumulative return?
A portfolio returns 7% and its relevant benchmark 5% for the same period. What is arithmetic active return?
questions.explanation: Subtract benchmark return from portfolio return on the same basis.

questions.question: A manager chooses a poorly performing benchmark only after seeing results. Why is this problematic?
questions.explanation: Benchmark selection should reflect the mandate, not hindsight.

questions.question: Return is 8%, risk-free rate 2%, volatility 12%. What is the simple Sharpe ratio?
questions.explanation: Excess return of 6% divided by volatility of 12% equals 0.5.

questions.question: A 95% one-day VaR estimate is $1m. Which interpretation is appropriate within the model?
options: Losses can exceed $1m on days outside the stated threshold
The portfolio is liquid by definition
questions.explanation: VaR is a probabilistic model threshold, not a worst-case cap.

questions.question: Attribution reports a positive allocation effect. What does that generally describe?
options: Proof every security selection was good
A guarantee of next year’s return
Value associated with portfolio weighting choices under the attribution method
questions.explanation: Allocation and selection are distinct contributors, defined by the chosen attribution framework.

glossary.definition: A resource with economic value.
An obligation owed to another party.
An ownership interest or the residual after liabilities.
The base amount invested or borrowed, excluding interest.
Gain or loss relative to an investment's starting value.
Price change plus income, expressed relative to starting value.
Return after accounting for inflation.
Return before an inflation adjustment.
Growth that includes earnings on prior earnings.
Today's equivalent of a future cash flow at a chosen discount rate.
The projected later value of money compounded at assumed rates.
The rate used to translate future cash flows into present value.
Discounted future net cash flows less the initial outlay.
The sum of values divided by their number.
The middle value in an ordered set.
A measure of dispersion around a mean.
The average squared deviation from a mean, under the chosen estimator.
A measure of linear association between variables.
A symmetric bell-shaped probability model.
A measure of the likelihood of an event.
A probability-weighted average of possible returns.
One hundredth of a percentage point.
The arithmetic difference between two percentages.
A security representing ownership in a company.
Residual company ownership, typically including voting rights.
Equity with specified priorities, often for distributions.
A distribution to shareholders, not guaranteed for common shares.
Share price multiplied by outstanding shares.
Earnings attributable to common shareholders per share, using the applicable share count.
Share price divided by earnings per share on a stated basis.
A change in share units that does not alone change total ownership value.
A debt security with contractual payment terms.
A bond's stated interest payment or rate.
The date a debt's principal is contractually due.
The face amount used in a security's contractual terms.
The discount rate equating a bond's price with promised cash flows through maturity.
A measure related to cash-flow timing and sensitivity to interest-rate changes.
Yields plotted against maturities for comparable debt.
Yield difference relative to a reference security or curve.
Failure to meet a contractual obligation.
A claim's priority relative to other claims.
Debt backed by specified collateral.
Debt without pledged specific collateral.
A bond the issuer may redeem early under specified terms.
A bond the holder may sell back under specified terms.
Debt convertible into equity under specified terms.
Debt without periodic coupons, often issued below face value.
Debt issued by state or local governmental entities; tax treatment varies.
Debt issued by the US Treasury.
Debt rated within the higher credit-quality categories of a rating scale.
Debt rated below investment grade, generally bearing greater credit risk.
Debt whose interest rate resets using a reference and specified terms.
A contract whose value depends on an underlying reference.
A customized agreement for a future transaction under specified terms.
A standardized exchange-traded contract for future transaction exposure.
A contract granting its buyer a right to buy under specified terms.
A contract granting its buyer a right to sell under specified terms.
The exercise price stated in an option contract.
The price paid by an option buyer.
A contract exchanging specified cash-flow streams.
A position intended to offset a risk exposure.
Use of borrowing or contracts to amplify economic exposure.
Ownership investments in companies outside public stock markets.
Property investments, held directly or through vehicles.
A physical economic good such as metal or agricultural output.
A real estate investment trust subject to jurisdiction-specific requirements.
A pooled vehicle using a specified strategy and often restricted access.
A pooled investment company whose investors own fund shares.
A pooled investment fund with shares traded on an exchange.
A fund seeking to track a specified index.
A fund investing primarily through other funds.
A fund structure with shares generally trading in a secondary market rather than daily investor redemption.
A closed-end structure offering periodic repurchases under its terms.
A mutual fund investing in short-term debt, not a bank deposit.
A fund whose asset mix typically evolves along a dated glide path.
The planned evolution of a portfolio's allocation over time.
A class of fund ownership with specified fees, eligibility or distribution arrangements.
Net asset value: assets minus liabilities, often stated per share.
Annual operating expenses expressed as a proportion of average fund assets.
A sales charge on fund purchase or redemption under its terms.
An offering document describing objectives, risks, fees and other key information.
An account managed under a client's mandate or agreement.
Separately managed account holding a client-specific portfolio.
The market for newly issued securities.
Trading of existing securities between investors.
An entity offering securities to raise capital.
An organized venue with rules for listing or trading.
Trading outside a centralized exchange, often through dealer networks.
The price a buyer offers for a security.
The price a seller requests for a security.
The difference between quoted ask and bid.
An instruction seeking execution at available market prices.
An instruction to trade only at a stated price or better.
Ease of transacting without substantial delay or price impact.
Determining and managing transaction obligations before settlement.
Completion of the exchange of assets and payment.
Exposure that generally benefits from a rise in the asset's value.
Exposure that generally benefits from a fall in the asset's value, with potentially substantial losses.
A reference used to assess a strategy or portfolio.
The division of a portfolio among categories of exposure.
Spreading exposures to reduce concentration, without eliminating loss risk.
Adjusting holdings back toward target weights.
Making portfolio choices intended to achieve a specified goal beyond simply tracking an index.
Managing primarily to follow a specified market or index exposure.
The willingness to accept uncertainty and losses.
Financial ability to withstand adverse outcomes.
The period before invested money is expected to be needed.
Investment policy statement documenting objectives, constraints and decision guidelines.
The standard deviation of returns relative to a benchmark.
A model-dependent estimate of return beyond what specified risk exposures explain.
Sensitivity of an investment's returns to a specified market factor.
Excess return relative to a risk-free rate per unit of return volatility.
Linked subperiod return designed to remove effects of external cash-flow timing.
Return measure incorporating the timing and amount of external cash flows.
Analysis separating contributors to portfolio results.
A modeled loss threshold for a chosen horizon and confidence level, not a maximum loss.
Potential losses from changes in market prices or rates.
Potential loss when an obligor does not meet its commitments.
Risk of being unable to transact when needed at acceptable prices.
Exposure to changes in foreign exchange rates.
Risk that purchasing power falls as prices rise.
Risk from failed processes, systems, people or external events.
Risk associated with failing applicable legal or regulatory requirements.
Risk that future cash flows must be reinvested at less favorable rates.
Risk from excessive dependence on a single exposure or correlated group.
Gross domestic product: production within an economy over a period.
A sustained increase in the general price level.
Central-bank actions affecting money and financial conditions.
Government decisions about taxation and spending.
Quantities sellers are willing and able to offer at different prices.
Quantities buyers are willing and able to purchase at different prices.
Responsiveness of one variable to a proportional change in another.
The value of the best alternative forgone.
Ability to produce at a lower opportunity cost.
The price of one currency in terms of another.
A statement of assets, liabilities and equity at a reporting date.
A report of revenue, expenses and profit over a period.
A report of operating, investing and financing cash movements.
Income recognized from business activities before associated expenses.
Recognizing economic events when earned or incurred rather than solely when cash moves.
Commonly current assets less current liabilities.
Allocation of a tangible asset's cost over its useful life.
An organization safeguarding assets and providing related administration.
A service provider maintaining ownership records and processing specified shareholder transactions.
A party owing legally defined duties to act for another's interests in a specified relationship.
A competing interest that can impair impartial judgment or duty.
Technology applied to financial services or processes.
Financial applications using decentralized networks, with material technical and governance risks.
An account through which securities can be held and traded.
An account without a retirement or other tax-advantaged wrapper; applicable income and gains may be taxed.
A brokerage account generally requiring payment in full rather than borrowing from the broker.
An account permitting borrowing against eligible securities under its terms.
An individual retirement arrangement with tax treatment subject to contribution, deduction and distribution rules.
An IRA with nondeductible contributions and potentially tax-free qualified withdrawals.
An IRA receiving an eligible transfer of retirement assets; rules depend on the source and method.
An IRA used in an employer-established simplified employee pension arrangement.
An employer retirement arrangement permitting employee salary reductions and required employer contributions.
An employer-sponsored defined-contribution plan with elective employee deferrals.
A retirement plan for eligible public-school, tax-exempt and certain other employees.
A deferred-compensation arrangement for eligible governmental or tax-exempt employers, with distinct rules.

coverageGaps: This maps the 23 topical modules in the publicly available 2026 syllabus. The public PDF is an outline, not the complete enrolled course or every private learning-outcome statement. No claim of exact outcome-by-outcome equivalence is made.
The official course, assigned activities and assessment requirements remain necessary. App scores are practice feedback, not a validated prediction of passing.
Detailed security valuation models, advanced derivatives mechanics, full probability calculations, jurisdiction-specific regulation and complete attribution formulas require deeper official study.
Account-type descriptions are a US-oriented supplement. They do not capture all tax rules, eligibility restrictions or current annual limits.
External videos are selected authoritative resources, not a verified video for every lesson; playback may require registration and links can change.
The first 60 questions retain their IDs; new questions extend the bank. Topic coverage is not weighted to an official assessment blueprint.

meta.scope: Independent introductory-to-applied companion with 50 original lessons and 150 original questions across the five topical courses in the 2026 public syllabus. Topic-level coverage of 23 syllabus modules is mapped, but this does not reproduce or replace the official curriculum, every learning outcome, exam questions or certification. Not CFA Level I preparation or a pass guarantee. US account glossary extends beyond the certificate. Educational only, not investment, legal or tax advice.
